mokha.name: Mokha
mokha.summary: A Red Sea port city in Yemen that was the principal port for Yemen's capital and, from the 16th to 19th centuries, the world's main marketplace for coffee, giving its name to 'mocha'.

al-ahsa-oasis.name: Al-Ahsa Oasis
al-ahsa-oasis.summary: An oasis and historical region in eastern Saudi Arabia made up of four cities, including Al-Hofuf and Al-Mubarraz, and 22 villages.

tihamah.name: Tihamah
tihamah.summary: The Red Sea coastal plain of the Arabian Peninsula, running from the Gulf of Aqaba to the Bab el Mandeb strait.

suleiman-the-magnificent.name: Suleiman the Magnificent
suleiman-the-magnificent.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, whose long reign brought the empire's greatest economic, military and political power and reformed its legal system.

ebussuud-efendi.name: Ebussuud Efendi
ebussuud-efendi.summary: Ottoman jurist and Quran scholar who served as Shaykh al-Islam of the Ottoman Empire from 1545 to 1574, working closely with Suleiman the Magnificent to reorganize Ottoman law.

bab-al-mandab-strait.name: Bab al-Mandab Strait
bab-al-mandab-strait.summary: A strategic strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean.

jer-nimo-lobo.name: Jerónimo Lobo
jer-nimo-lobo.summary: A Portuguese Jesuit missionary (1595–1678) who tried to convert Ethiopia to Roman Catholicism until the Jesuits' expulsion in 1643, later writing an important account of his time there.

sanaa.name: Sanaa
sanaa.summary: Capital and largest city of Yemen, at 2,300 metres in the Sarawat Mountains, with an Old City that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

pasha.name: Pasha
pasha.summary: A high-rank Ottoman title granted by the Sultan to governors, generals and dignitaries, roughly equivalent to a British Lord; also used in Egypt and Morocco.

abyssinia.name: Abyssinia
abyssinia.summary: A historical name for a region in the Horn of Africa, roughly modern Ethiopia and Eritrea, used internationally as a synonym for Ethiopia until the mid-20th century.

amiriya-madrasa.name: Amiriya Madrasa
amiriya-madrasa.summary: A 16th-century madrasa in Rada, Yemen, built in 1504 as an example of Tahirid architecture, and restored over two decades by archaeologist Selma Al-Radi after falling into disrepair.

radda-district.name: Rada'a district
radda-district.summary: A district of Yemen's Al Bayda Governorate whose largest city, Rada'a, is known for its 16th-century Amiriya Madrasa and mosque.

shibam.name: Shibam
shibam.summary: A walled town in eastern Yemen founded around the 3rd century, famed for centuries-old mudbrick high-rises up to eleven stories, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

great-mosque-of-sanaa.name: Great Mosque of Sanaa
great-mosque-of-sanaa.summary: One of the oldest mosques in the world, said to have been founded around 633 CE in Sanaa, Yemen, built partly from materials taken from an earlier palace and church on the site.

ablaq.name: Ablaq
ablaq.summary: Architectural technique of alternating rows of light and dark stone used decoratively in Islamic architecture, possibly derived from earlier Byzantine building methods in the region.

al-mahdi-mosque-sanaa.name: Al-Mahdi Mosque, Sanaa
al-mahdi-mosque-sanaa.summary: A historic mosque in the old city of Sana'a, Yemen, built in 1651, forming part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site there.

al-mahdi-abbas.name: Al-Mahdi Abbas
al-mahdi-abbas.summary: An Imam of Yemen (1719-1775) who ruled from 1748 to 1775, a member of the Qasimid family descended from the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

aden.name: Aden
aden.summary: Ancient port city on Yemen's south coast, at the eastern approach to the Red Sea, serving since 2014 as the de facto capital of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

al-bakiriyya-mosque.name: Al-Bakiriyya Mosque
al-bakiriyya-mosque.summary: A mosque built in Sana'a around 1596-97 by the Ottoman governor of Yemen, later restored after falling into disrepair when the Ottomans were driven out.

selim-i.name: Selim I
selim-i.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1512 to 1520, known as Selim the Grim, whose conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the Levant made the Ottoman Empire the leading Muslim power.

hejaz.name: Hejaz
hejaz.summary: A historical region of western Arabia, in modern Saudi Arabia, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, the first and second holiest sites in Islam.

asir.name: Asir
asir.summary: A province in southern Saudi Arabia bordering Yemen, with Abha as its capital and a population of about 2 million.

muqrin-ibn-zamil.name: Muqrin ibn Zamil
muqrin-ibn-zamil.summary: Last Jabrid ruler of Bahrain and eastern Arabia, defeated and mortally wounded by an invading Portuguese force that conquered Bahrain in 1521.

qatif.name: Qatif
qatif.summary: One of the oldest settlements in Arabia, with a history dating to 3500 BC, historically known to the Sumerians as Dilmun and now part of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province.

al-muntafiq.name: Al-Muntafiq
al-muntafiq.summary: A large Arab tribal confederation and semi-centralized emirate of southern Iraq and Kuwait, with a mix of Sunni and Shia tribes, that lost formal recognition once Ottoman rule ended.

bani-khalid-tribe.name: Bani Khalid
bani-khalid-tribe.summary: An Arab tribal confederation that ruled southern Iraq, Kuwait and Eastern Arabia from the 15th to 18th century, later under Ottoman protection.

sharif-of-mecca.name: Sharif of Mecca
sharif-of-mecca.summary: The title of the traditional steward of Mecca and Medina, charged with protecting the cities and pilgrims, an office dating back to the late Abbasid era into the 20th century.

najd.name: Najd
najd.summary: A historical central region of the Arabian Peninsula, home to about a third of Saudi Arabia's population and to the House of Saud.

diriyah.name: Diriyah
diriyah.summary: Town near Riyadh that was the original home of the House of Saud and capital of the first Saudi state from 1727 to 1818; its old district is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

jabrids.name: Jabrids
jabrids.summary: An Arab dynasty that ruled nearly all of Arabia along with parts of Oman and Yemen, extending into Iran's southern coast and control of the Strait of Hormuz.

kingdom-of-hormuz.name: Kingdom of Hormuz
kingdom-of-hormuz.summary: A trading kingdom on the Persian Gulf founded in the 11th century by a dynasty of Arab origin, controlling a key port between the Gulf and the Indian Ocean until becoming a Portuguese client state.

qasida.name: Qasida
qasida.summary: An ancient Arabic ode form using a single meter and rhyme throughout, originating in pre-Islamic poetry and later adopted into Persian and Turkish literature.

imru-al-qais.name: Imru' al-Qais
imru-al-qais.summary: Pre-Islamic Arabian poet from Najd, active in the late 5th and early 6th centuries and the last king of Kinda, often called the father of Arabic poetry.

ras-al-khaimah.name: Ras Al Khaimah
ras-al-khaimah.summary: Port city and capital of the emirate of the same name in the UAE, successor to the historic Islamic-era trading hub of Julfar.

al-mansur-al-qasim.name: Al-Mansur al-Qasim
al-mansur-al-qasim.summary: An Imam of Yemen known as 'the Great' (1559-1620) who led the struggle to free Yemen from Ottoman rule and founded a Zaidi kingdom that lasted until 1970.

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

muhammad-bin-saud-al-muqrin.name: Muhammad bin Saud
muhammad-bin-saud-al-muqrin.summary: Emir of Diriyah from 1727 to 1765, considered the founder of the First Saudi State and the Saud dynasty.

wahhabism.name: Wahhabism
wahhabism.summary: A Salafi revivalist movement within Sunni Islam named after the 18th-century scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, originating in Najd and later spreading across the Arabian Peninsula.

custodian-of-the-two-holy-mosques.name: Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques
custodian-of-the-two-holy-mosques.summary: Royal title claiming responsibility for guarding Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities; historically used by rulers including the Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans, and by Saudi monarchs since 1986.
custodian-of-the-two-holy-mosques.source_title: Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques

taif.name: Taif
taif.summary: A city in the Hejaz mountains of Saudi Arabia, visited by the Prophet Muhammad in the early 7th century and long inhabited by the Banu Thaqif tribe.

bani-khalid-emirate.name: Barrak ibn Ghurayr
bani-khalid-emirate.summary: Bani Khalid emir who founded the Bani Khalid Emirate in 1669 by driving Ottoman forces from Al-Ahsa and made his capital at Al-Mubarraz.

muhammad-ibn-abd-al-wahhab.name: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab
muhammad-ibn-abd-al-wahhab.summary: Arab Muslim scholar and preacher (1703–1792) from Najd who called for a return to the Quran and Hadith over traditional interpretation and is considered the founder of the Wahhabi movement.

uyayna.name: Uyayna
uyayna.summary: A village near Riyadh in central Saudi Arabia, the birthplace of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, founder of the Wahhabi religious movement.

house-of-saud.name: House of Saud
house-of-saud.summary: The ruling royal family of Saudi Arabia, descended from Muhammad bin Saud, founder of the 18th-century Emirate of Diriyah, and today among the wealthiest families in the world.

ajwad-ibn-zamil.name: Ajwad ibn Zamil
ajwad-ibn-zamil.summary: Ruler of the Jabrids (1418–1496) who in the late 15th century united most of Eastern Arabia under a single state.

al-nasir-muhammad.name: al-Nasir Muhammad
al-nasir-muhammad.summary: Ninth Mamluk sultan of the Bahri dynasty, ruling Egypt across three reigns between 1293 and 1341, who reformed taxation and appointed loyal officials to fight corruption.

first-saudi-state.name: First Saudi State
first-saudi-state.summary: Arabian polity from 1744 to 1818, also called the Emirate of Diriyah, founded by an alliance between Muhammad bin Saud and religious reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab.

huraymila.name: Huraymila
huraymila.summary: A governorate in Riyadh Province, Saudi Arabia, in the northwestern part of the province.

al-mubarraz.name: Al-Mubarraz
al-mubarraz.summary: A city in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia, that served as the district's ruling center from 1669 to 1793, before Saudi rule began.

saud-bin-muhammad-al-muqrin.name: Saud I
saud-bin-muhammad-al-muqrin.summary: 13th emir of the Sheikhdom of Diriyah (1640–1725), known as Saud I, and founder of the House of Saud; his son Muhammad bin Saud later founded the First Saudi State.

taqlid.name: Taqlid
taqlid.summary: An Islamic legal term for conforming to the teaching of another rather than reasoning independently; in Salafi usage it is criticized as "blind imitation."

ibrahim-al-kurani.name: Ibrahim al-Kurani
ibrahim-al-kurani.summary: A 17th-century Islamic scholar and theologian (1616–1690) of the Shafi'i school who was a proponent of Wahdat al-Wujud before adhering to Atharism, and taught prominent ulama including Abd al-Rauf al-Fansuri and Yusuf al-Makassari.

ahmad-al-qushashi.name: Ahmad al-Qushashi
ahmad-al-qushashi.summary: Sufi master of the Shattariyya order, born in Medina in 1583, who taught it in a more Sharia-oriented way and whose students spread it across Southeast Asia.

prophet-s-mosque.name: Prophet's Mosque
prophet-s-mosque.summary: The second mosque built by Muhammad, in Medina, and the second holiest site in Islam after Mecca's Masjid al-Haram, originally serving as a community center, court, and school.

the-people-of-monotheism.name: Muwahhidun
the-people-of-monotheism.summary: Arabic term meaning 'the monotheists,' used by the 18th-century Arabian revivalist movement of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab to describe its own followers.

ibn-taymiyya.name: Ibn Taymiyya
ibn-taymiyya.summary: A Sunni Muslim scholar and jurist (1263–1328) born in Harran, whose creedal treatises later became a key reference for the Salafi movement, despite being censored and imprisoned in his lifetime.

hanbali-school.name: Hanbali school
hanbali-school.summary: The smallest of the four major Sunni schools of Islamic law, based on Ahmad ibn Hanbal's teachings and later linked to the 18th-century Wahhabi movement.

ijtihad.name: Ijtihad
ijtihad.summary: Independent reasoning by a qualified Islamic legal scholar to resolve a legal question, contrasted with simply following precedent; a scholar entitled to practice it is called a mujtahid.

wahdat-al-wuj-d.name: Wahdat al-Wujud
wahdat-al-wuj-d.summary: An Islamic mystical doctrine holding that God is identical with existence itself, attributed to the Sufi Ibn Arabi (d. 1240) and later popular among Sufis despite being condemned by some scholars as heretical.

ibn-arabi.name: Ibn Arabi
ibn-arabi.summary: An Andalusian Sufi mystic, poet and philosopher (1165–1240) whose vast writings, especially on the 'unity of existence,' became a dominant framework across the Muslim world.

atharism.name: Atharism
atharism.summary: School of Sunni theology favoring strict, literal interpretation of the Quran and hadith over rational disputation, which coalesced under Ahmad ibn Hanbal (780 to 855).

rassid-dynasty.name: Rassid dynasty
rassid-dynasty.summary: Zaidi Shia dynasty of imams that ruled parts of Yemen from 897, blending religious and political authority until the monarchy's abolition in 1970.

taqiyya.name: Taqiyya
taqiyya.summary: The Islamic practice of concealing one's faith to avoid danger, mainly associated with Shia Islam but also permitted under certain conditions in Sunni tradition.

al-ash-sheikh.name: Al ash-Sheikh
al-ash-sheikh.summary: Saudi Arabia's leading religious family, descended from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, second only to the Al Saud royal family, with whom it has shared power for nearly 300 years.

gargee-an.name: Gargee'an
gargee-an.summary: A centuries-old Eastern Arabian holiday held twice during Ramadan and Sha'ban, when children in traditional dress go door-to-door singing for sweets.

enjoining-good-and-forbidding-wrong.name: Enjoining good and forbidding wrong
enjoining-good-and-forbidding-wrong.summary: Islamic duty from the Quran and Hadith to intervene and enforce Islamic law, underlying the classical institution of hisba and modern religious-police bodies.
